Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
620 AM EST Sat Nov 14 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 206 AM EST Saturday...

No significant changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 206 AM EST Saturday...

1. Widespread upslope snow showers today, gradually tapering 
off Sunday. 

2. A warm, dry and mostly sunny week is in store.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 206 AM EST Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Cyclonic northwest flow will prevail under an upper- 
level low this weekend. A potent embedded shortwave will pass south 
today and tonight, bringing widespread showers. While they will be 
most concentrated in the typical northwest flow upslope areas, very 
marginal instability will develop in the lowest 10,000 ft in the 
atmosphere due to cold air aloft and solar heating. This will cause 
the precipitation to trend more convective, especially this 
afternoon. Therefore, snow showers will be able to survive crossing 
the terrain and should pass through the downslope areas like the 
Connecticut River Valley, though likely in a lighter form. While 
temperatures will rise above freezing below 2,000 ft and likely 
reach 40 in the lowest points, temperatures will drop significantly 
in any of the showers. Therefore, even though consistent snow levels 
will likely only be down to around 1,000-1,500 ft, a period of 
graupel or even brief wet snow will be possible all the way down 
into the valleys. However, any continuous accumulations should 
generally be limited to above 2,000 ft. The showers will gradually 
become less and less widespread heading into Sunday, and they should 
be done by Sunday evening. Accumulations by the end should be in the 
1-4 inch range above 2,000 ft, with mostly brief coatings that melt 
below that. The lowest accumulating snow levels will be tonight. 
Moisture off Lake Champlain will enhance the showers in parts of the 
Champlain Valley and Greens, but the more convective nature may 
prevent the formation of distinct bands at times.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A potent ridge and associated area of surface high 
pressure will dominate the weather next week, making it feel as if 
it were still mid-October. In a classic El Nino pattern, deep 
troughing and strong surface lows over the Pacific have caused 
continuous southwest to westerly flow out west, flooding the Great 
Plains and western Canada with warm Pacific air. This has caused 
temperature anomalies in the 20-30+ degree range. This airmass will 
begin to arrive Monday, but clouds will likely remain stuck under 
the inversion, so it will likely take until Tuesday to warm up. From 
then through the end of the week, and potentially through the 
weekend, highs in the 50s will prevail, though 60 will be possible 
in some of the warmest areas. There will be a strong, persistent 
subsidence inversion, and it will aided by the fact that 
significantly more surface heat will be lost at night than will be 
able to be replenished by the sun during the day. Radiational 
cooling will help lows drop to the 20s and 30s, around 
climatological normals. Weak troughs will gradually erode the ridge 
from the north, but it will take until at least next weekend for it 
to get pushed to the south and east and for cooler conditions and 
chances for precipitation to return.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 12Z Sunday...A mix of flight categories currently exist due
to low ceilings and they will generally hold steady for the next few
hours. Heading into the late morning and afternoon, ceilings should
increase a bit but they will likely remain a mix of MVFR and VFR.
Ceilings will mostly decrease into the MVFR range tonight. Scattered
showers will continue through the evening, falling mostly as snow,
but some rain should mix in at BTV and PBG. During the day, some
intervals of MVFR or IFR visibility will occur at every terminal,
with the most at SLK and EFK. At those terminals, it should be
relatively steady. Temperatures above freezing during the day should
prevent much accumulation on runways. While lingering snow showers
are possible tonight, they should be mostly restricted to SLK and
EFK. Northwest Wind gusts in the 5-15 KT range are expected during
the day and they should generally drop under 10 KT at night.

Outlook...

Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Slight chance SHSN.
Sunday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
